issues.issue: The effective date is written as an illegible, incomplete entry ("Aust { i 997"), so the date the Agreement takes effect cannot be read off the instrument. A missing or unreadable commencement date is a mechanical defect that changes what the clause does.
The 1997 effective date contradicts the preamble, which recites that the Agreement is made on a day in 1999, leaving the instrument with two irreconcilable start dates.

"Certified securities" appears to be an error for "certificated securities", and the clause gives the Custodian an unqualified election between segregation and fungible bulk without saying who chooses. "Held either separate from the securities of the Custodian and all of its other customers" is also ambiguous as to whether both separations are required.

The unqualified statement that securities "shall be withdrawable upon the demand of the Owner" sits against Section 6, which lets the Custodian withhold assets for outstanding fees and "balances owing", so the only stated exception (Commissioner-controlled deposits) is not in fact the only one.

The examination right is conditioned "only upon furnishing the Custodian with written instructions to that effect from an appropriate officer of the Owner", and "appropriate officer" and "appropriate regulatory body" are both undefined. The proviso can also be read to condition even a regulator's access on the Owner's written instruction.

The conditions and limits here contradict Section 9 (Inspection Privileges), which subjects the Custodian's books, records and practices to examination by the Owner with no notice, premises or written-instruction requirement.

The trailing qualifier "that the Owner may reasonably request" may modify only limb (b) or both limbs, deciding whether clearing-corporation control reports must be sent automatically or only on request. The syntax leaves that genuinely open.

The indemnity is confined to "loss of custodied securities" occasioned by an enumerated list ending in "mysterious disappearance, including loss by damage or destruction", so whether it reaches economic loss short of physical loss of the securities is open. The enumerated causes invite an ejusdem generis reading of "mysterious disappearance".

Its allocation of loss caused by Custodian negligence runs against Section 7, under which the Owner indemnifies the Custodian for "any and all claims" incurred by reason of its acting as Custodian, subject only to the Section 7 negligence carve-out.

"Shall promptly replace the securities or the value thereof" does not say who elects between replacement in kind and payment of value, nor how "value" or "the value of any loss of rights or privileges" is measured or as of what date.

The excusing events end in the catch-alls "other differences with employees" and "or similar causes beyond its reasonable control", whose reach against the enumerated specifics is exactly the ejusdem generis question; "lot" is also an obvious error for "riot". Whether "laws, regulations, orders" is itself an excusing event or merely a governmental-act example is left unclear by the punctuation.

The proviso lets a non-party, the Insurance Commissioner of the state of domicile, accept "a standard of liability applicable to the agent that is different from" the Custodian's, without saying when, how or with what effect on the Owner's rights. "May accept" leaves it unclear whether the different standard ever becomes contractually operative.

It undercuts the immediately preceding requirement in Section 24 that the agent be subject to "the same liability for loss of custodied securities as the Custodian", so the same section both requires and dispenses with parity of liability.

"Insurance protection consistent with the requirements of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency" identifies no policy, limit or requirement, and the OCC prescribes no fixed custodial insurance standard. The measure of compliance with the warranty is therefore indeterminate.
